title: Curvilinear Coordinates
summary: Many problems have a natural shape: a circle, a cylinder, a sphere. In such problems Cartesian coordinates make the formulas ugly. In this chapter we derive the gradient, divergence, curl and Laplacian in any orthogonal coordinate system, and then read off…

intro.x: Many problems have a natural shape: a circle, a cylinder, a sphere. In such problems Cartesian coordinates make the formulas ugly. In this chapter we derive the gradient, divergence, curl and Laplacian in any orthogonal coordinate system, and then read off the formulas for cylindrical and spherical coordinates. The proofs use only the identities of Chapter 3.

blocks.x: Let $(u_1,u_2,u_3)\mapsto\vec r(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ be a $C^2$ map with invertible Jacobian, so that each point of space (in a region) has coordinates $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$. The curves obtained by changing one $u_i$ and keeping the others fixed are the coordinate curves; the surfaces $u_i=\text{const}$ are the coordinate surfaces.
The vector $\partial\vec r/\partial u_i$ is tangent to the $u_i$-coordinate curve. Its length is the scale factor
h_i=\Bigl\lVert\pd{\vec r}{u_i}\Bigr\rVert,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\ehat_i=\frac1{h_i}\pd{\vec r}{u_i}

is the unit basis vector. The coordinate system is orthogonal if $\ehat_1,\ehat_2,\ehat_3$ are perpendicular at every point; we also assume they are right-handed, so that $\ehat_1\times\ehat_2=\ehat_3$ (and cyclically).
The scale factor $h_i$ answers the question: if $u_i$ changes by $\dd u_i$, how far do we move? The answer is $h_i\,\dd u_i$.

For cylindrical coordinates, $\vec r=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)$, so $\partial_r\vec r=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$ (length $1$), $\partial_\theta\vec r=(-r\sin\theta,r\cos\theta,0)$ (length $r$), and $\partial_z\vec r=\khat$. The spherical case was computed in Theorem 4.9.

blocks.caption: Polar coordinates. Blue circles are curves of constant $r$; orange rays are curves of constant $\theta$. The basis vectors $\ehat_r$ (radially outward) and $\ehat_\theta$ (counterclockwise) are perpendicular but point in different directions at different places. This is the main difference from Cartesian coordinates.

blocks.x: By the chain rule, a small change $(\dd u_1,\dd u_2,\dd u_3)$ moves the point by
\dd\vec r=\sum_i\pd{\vec r}{u_i}\dd u_i=h_1\dd u_1\,\ehat_1+h_2\dd u_2\,\ehat_2+h_3\dd u_3\,\ehat_3 .
Because the $\ehat_i$ are orthonormal, we read off:
Surface element on the surface $u_3=\text{const}$: $\dd S=h_1h_2\,\dd u_1\dd u_2$ (and similarly for the others).
Volume element: $\dd V=h_1h_2h_3\,\dd u_1\dd u_2\dd u_3$.
The volume element agrees with Theorem 4.8: the Jacobian matrix has orthogonal rows $h_i\ehat_i$, so $\abs{\det}=h_1h_2h_3$.

On the sphere $\rho=R$, the surface element is $\dd S=h_\varphi h_\theta\,\dd\varphi\,\dd\theta=R\cdot R\sin\varphi\,\dd\varphi\,\dd\theta=R^2\sin\varphi\,\dd\varphi\,\dd\theta$. Total area $=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi R^2\sin\varphi\,\dd\varphi\,\dd\theta=4\pi R^2$. On the cylinder $r=R$: $\dd S=R\,\dd\theta\,\dd z$.

Let $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ be a right-handed orthogonal coordinate system of class $C^2$ with scale factors $h_i$. Write $\partial_i=\partial/\partial u_i$, let $f$ be a $C^2$ scalar field and let $\vec F=F_1\ehat_1+F_2\ehat_2+F_3\ehat_3$ be a $C^1$ vector field. Then

Gradient. By the chain rule, $\partial_if= abla f\cdot\partial_i\vec r=h_i\, abla f\cdot\ehat_i$. Hence $ abla f\cdot\ehat_i=\partial_if/h_i$. Since $(\ehat_i)$ is an orthonormal basis, $ abla f=\sum_i( abla f\cdot\ehat_i)\ehat_i$, which is the formula. Applying it to the coordinate function $f=u_i$ (so $\partial_ju_i=\delta_{ij}$) gives
\nabla u_i=\frac1{h_i}\ehat_i,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\ehat_i=h_i\nabla u_i .\tag{$\dagger$}
Divergence. Consider the term $F_1\ehat_1$. Since $\ehat_1=\ehat_2\times\ehat_3$, ($\dagger$) gives $\ehat_1=h_2h_3\,\nabla u_2\times\nabla u_3$, so
F_1\ehat_1=g\,\nabla u_2\times\nabla u_3\qquad\text{with }g=h_2h_3F_1 .

Using $\ehat_2\times\ehat_1=-\ehat_3$ and $\ehat_3\times\ehat_1=\ehat_2$,
\curl(F_1\ehat_1)=\frac1{h_1h_3}\partial_3(h_1F_1)\,\ehat_2-\frac1{h_1h_2}\partial_2(h_1F_1)\,\ehat_3 .

Adding the two cyclic analogues, the coefficient of $\ehat_1$ is $\frac1{h_2h_3}\bigl[\partial_2(h_3F_3)-\partial_3(h_2F_2)\bigr]$, and similarly for $\ehat_2,\ehat_3$. This is exactly the expansion of the determinant in the statement.
Laplacian. $\lap f=\divg\nabla f$. Apply the divergence formula to the field with components $F_i=\partial_if/h_i$:
\lap f=\frac1{h_1h_2h_3}\sum_i\partial_i\Bigl(\frac{h_jh_k}{h_i}\,\partial_if\Bigr),
where $(i,j,k)$ runs over cyclic permutations of $(1,2,3)$.
Cylindrical $(r,\theta,z)$, with $\vec F=F_r\ehat_r+F_\theta\ehat_\theta+F_z\ehat_z$:
Spherical $(\rho,\varphi,\theta)$, with $\vec F=F_\rho\ehat_\rho+F_\varphi\ehat_\varphi+F_\theta\ehat_\theta$:

Insert $(h_1,h_2,h_3)=(1,r,1)$, respectively $(1,\rho,\rho\sin\varphi)$, into Theorem 5.4. For example, for the spherical divergence: $h_2h_3=\rho^2\sin\varphi$, $h_3h_1=\rho\sin\varphi$, $h_1h_2=\rho$, $h_1h_2h_3=\rho^2\sin\varphi$, so
\divg\vec F=\frac1{\rho^2\sin\varphi}\Bigl[\partial_\rho(\rho^2\sin\varphi\,F_\rho)+\partial_\varphi(\rho\sin\varphi\,F_\varphi)+\partial_\theta(\rho F_\theta)\Bigr],
and dividing through (the factors $\sin\varphi$, $\rho$ do not depend on the variable of differentiation in the first and third terms) gives the stated form.
Inverse-square field. $\vec F=\rho^{-2}\ehat_\rho$: $\rho^2F_\rho=1$ is constant, so $\divg\vec F=0$ for $\rho>0$.

Radial Laplacian. If $f=f(\rho)$, then $\lap f=\rho^{-2}(\rho^2f')'=f''+\tfrac2\rho f'$. The solutions of $\lap f=0$ are $f=A+B/\rho$, in agreement with Chapter 3. In the plane, $f=f(r)$: $\lap f=\frac1r(rf')'$ with solutions $A+B\ln r$.
Rigid rotation. $\vec F=\omega r\,\ehat_\theta$ (in cylindrical coordinates): $\curl\vec F=\frac1r\partial_r(r\cdot\omega r)\ehat_z=2\omega\,\ehat_z$, as in Theorem 3.8.
The vortex $\vec G=\dfrac1r\ehat_\theta$ $(=(-y,x)/(x^2+y^2))$: $\curl\vec G=\frac1r\partial_r(r\cdot\frac1r)\ehat_z=0$ and $\divg\vec G=\frac1r\partial_\theta(\frac1r)=0$.

In curvilinear coordinates, $\lap\vec F\ne(\lap F_1)\ehat_1+(\lap F_2)\ehat_2+(\lap F_3)\ehat_3$. The basis vectors depend on position, so they must be differentiated too. The component-wise rule holds only in Cartesian coordinates. For a vector field, use $\lap\vec F=\nabla(\divg\vec F)-\curl\curl\vec F$ (Theorem 3.15(7)). Likewise, $\divg$ of $\vec F$ is not $\sum\partial_iF_i$ in these coordinates: the scale factors enter.

In Cartesian coordinates, $\ihat,\jhat,\khat$ are constant, so differentiating a vector field means differentiating its components. In polar coordinates, $\ehat_r=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and $\ehat_\theta=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$, so
\pd{\ehat_r}\theta=\ehat_\theta,\qquad\pd{\ehat_\theta}\theta=-\ehat_r,\qquad\pd{\ehat_r}r=\pd{\ehat_\theta}r=\vec 0 .
These formulas are the source of the extra terms in curvilinear derivatives.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Velocity and acceleration in polar coordinates

blocks.x: For a particle with position $\vec r(t)=r(t)\,\ehat_r$ (with $r=r(t)$, $\theta=\theta(t)$),

By the chain rule $\dot{\ehat}_r=\dot\theta\,\ehat_\theta$ and $\dot{\ehat}_\theta=-\dot\theta\,\ehat_r$. Then $\vec v=\frac{\dd}{\dd t}(r\ehat_r)=\dot r\ehat_r+r\dot\theta\ehat_\theta$. Differentiating again,

\vec a=\ddot r\ehat_r+\dot r\dot\theta\ehat_\theta+(\dot r\dot\theta+r\ddot\theta)\ehat_\theta+r\dot\theta(-\dot\theta\ehat_r)=(\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2)\ehat_r+(r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta)\ehat_\theta .

The term $-r\dot\theta^2\,\ehat_r$ is the centripetal acceleration: a particle moving on a circle ($r$ constant) at angular speed $\dot\theta$ accelerates towards the centre with magnitude $r\dot\theta^2=v^2/r$. The term $2\dot r\dot\theta\,\ehat_\theta$ is the Coriolis term. If the central force is $F(r)\ehat_r$, the $\ehat_\theta$-equation is $\frac{\dd}{\dd t}(r^2\dot\theta)=0$: angular momentum is conserved (Kepler’s second law).

blocks.caption: The local frame $(\ehat_\rho,\ehat_\varphi,\ehat_\theta)$ of spherical coordinates at a point $P$. $\ehat_\rho$ points away from the origin, $\ehat_\varphi$ points “south” (increasing polar angle) and $\ehat_\theta$ points “east” (increasing azimuth). The three are mutually perpendicular and right-handed. At a different point, the frame points in different directions.

blocks.x: Scale factors $h_i=\norm{\partial\vec r/\partial u_i}$; $\dd\vec r=\sum h_i\dd u_i\ehat_i$; $\dd V=h_1h_2h_3\,\dd u_1\dd u_2\dd u_3$.
Cylindrical $(1,r,1)$; spherical $(1,\rho,\rho\sin\varphi)$.
$\nabla f=\sum\frac1{h_i}\partial_if\,\ehat_i$; $\divg\vec F=\frac1{h_1h_2h_3}\sum\partial_i(h_jh_kF_i)$; $\lap f=\frac1{h_1h_2h_3}\sum\partial_i\bigl(\frac{h_jh_k}{h_i}\partial_if\bigr)$.
Proof idea: $\ehat_i=h_i\nabla u_i$, and then $\curl\nabla=0$, $\divg\curl=0$ and the product rules do the work.
Basis vectors change from point to point: $\partial_\theta\ehat_r=\ehat_\theta$, $\partial_\theta\ehat_\theta=-\ehat_r$. This gives centripetal and Coriolis terms.
Never apply $\lap$ component-wise to a vector field outside Cartesian coordinates.
What is a scale factor? The length change per unit change of a coordinate: $h_i=\norm{\partial\vec r/\partial u_i}$. For $\theta$ in polar coordinates, $h=r$.
Write the Laplacian in polar coordinates. $\lap f=\frac1r\partial_r(r\partial_rf)+\frac1{r^2}\partial_\theta^2f$.
Why does $\divg\vec F$ in spherical coordinates contain $\rho^2F_\rho$ and not $F_\rho$? Flux through a sphere of radius $\rho$ is $F_\rho\cdot4\pi\rho^2$: the area grows like $\rho^2$.
Derive the acceleration in polar coordinates. Differentiate $r\ehat_r$ using $\dot{\ehat}_r=\dot\theta\ehat_\theta$, $\dot{\ehat}_\theta=-\dot\theta\ehat_r$.
Why is $\lap\vec F\ne\lap$ of its components in cylindrical coordinates? The basis vectors $\ehat_r,\ehat_\theta$ depend on $\theta$.
Exercises

Compute the scale factors of parabolic cylindrical coordinates $\vec r=\bigl(\tfrac12(u^2-v^2),\,uv,\,z\bigr)$, check orthogonality, and write the Laplacian. (Answer: $h_u=h_v=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$, $h_z=1$.)
Derive the spherical curl formula’s $\ehat_\rho$-component, $\dfrac1{\rho\sin\varphi}\Bigl[\partial_\varphi(\sin\varphi\,F_\theta)-\partial_\theta F_\varphi\Bigr]$, from Theorem 5.4.
Show that $f=\ln r$ in $\R^2$ and $f=1/\rho$ in $\R^3$ are the only radial harmonic functions (up to $A+B f$), by solving the radial ODEs.
Using Theorem 5.7, show that if the force on a particle is central ($\vec F\parallel\ehat_r$) then $r^2\dot\theta$ is constant. Interpret $\tfrac12r^2\dot\theta$ as the area swept per unit time.

Compute the surface area of the cone $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ for $0\le z\le h$ using the scale factors of cylindrical coordinates (area element on the surface $z=r$: the surface is parametrized by $(r,\theta)$ with $\partial_r\vec r=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,1)$ of length $\sqrt2$). (Answer: $\sqrt2\,\pi h^2$.)
